intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that B-cell immunodeficiency, distal limb anomalies, and urogenital malformations (BILU), also known as Hoffman syndrome, is caused by heterozygous mutation in the TOP2B gene (126431) on chromosome 3p24.

checks.explanation: Paper equates BILU and Hoffman syndromes.

checks.claim: BILU/Hoffman syndrome is caused by heterozygous mutation in the TOP2B gene.
checks.evidence_quote: In three families with Hoffman syndrome,, we identified three heterozygous mutations affecting the TOPRIM, or DNA gating, domain of the type II topoisomerase TOP2B.
checks.explanation: The paper attributes Hoffman syndrome to heterozygous TOP2B mutations.

checks.claim: The TOP2B gene is located on chromosome 3p24.
checks.evidence_quote: One gene, TOP2B, which encodes topoisomerase IIβ, was affected by a heterozygous variant in each family
checks.explanation: The gene identified is TOP2B; the cytogenetic location 3p24 is standard nomenclature for that approved gene symbol, though the paper itself does not state the locus.

paragraphs.text: BILU syndrome, also called Hoffman syndrome, is an autosomal dominant syndromic B-cell immunodeficiency. Affected individuals have agammaglobulinemia or hypogammaglobulinemia with absent or reduced B cells, together with facial dysmorphism, distal limb anomalies, and urogenital malformations. T-cell and myeloid lineages are normal.

checks.explanation: Autosomal dominant syndromic B-cell immunodeficiency, later named Hoffman syndrome, is exactly as described.

checks.explanation: Patients had agammaglobulinemia/hypogammaglobulinemia, and the paper documents absent CD19+ B cells with reduced but detectable immunoglobulins.

paragraphs.text: Hoffman et al. (2001) reported a 6-year-old girl with an isolated humoral immune deficiency and a unique combination of dysmorphic features. Physical findings included microcephaly, micrognathia, sickle-shaped eyebrows, hypoplastic alae nasi, thenar hypoplasia, partial syndactyly of toes 4 and 5, recessed great toes, anterior anus, and hypoplastic labia minora. She also had triphalangeal thumbs, hypoplastic first metatarsals, postnatal growth retardation, and developmental delay; her development was substantially slower than that of her twin. She had recurrent sinopulmonary infections and pneumococcal bacteremia. Laboratory evaluation showed hypogammaglobulinemia, absent B cells, and a 46,XX karyotype. A review of the literature and the London Dysmorphology Database found no recognizable syndrome that matched her findings, and the authors suggested that she might represent a unique syndrome of unknown etiology.

paragraphs.text: Broderick et al. (2019) studied 3 families with Hoffman syndrome. Two of them were unrelated families with autosomal dominant syndromic B-cell immunodeficiency that the authors had reported previously. Ages at presentation were 7 and 35 years in family 1 and 6 years in family 2. The probands presented with recurrent infections by polysaccharide-encapsulated bacteria, severe hypogammaglobulinemia, and absent CD19+ B cells, and they had facial dysmorphism and limb anomalies. T-cell responses to mitogens were normal. The patient in the third family presented at 5 years of age. This patient had initially been reported as having an atypical presentation of ablepharon-macrostomia syndrome and was later found to have humoral immunodeficiency. The patients had normal numbers of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells but no detectable peripheral B cells, and NK cells were reduced in 2 of them. The patients did not form germinal centers and did not generate protective serologic titers to immunization (tetanus, diphtheria, H. influenzae B). However, detectable amounts of circulating immunoglobulins indicated that some B cells were present below the clinical limits of detection. Malignancy was not observed in the patients.

paragraphs.text: Broderick et al. (2019) performed whole-genome sequencing of affected and unaffected members of 2 unrelated families with Hoffman syndrome. In each family they found a heterozygous variant in the TOP2B gene that was present only in affected members: a de novo in-frame deletion (c.1761_1763delAGA, p.EE587E) and a missense mutation (c.1448C-T, S483L). Independent reanalysis of clinical whole-exome sequencing data from the patient in a third family revealed a heterozygous c.1897G-A transition in TOP2B, resulting in a gly633-to-ser (G633S) substitution. All 3 mutations affected the TOPRIM (DNA gating) domain and were confirmed by Sanger sequencing. The authors noted that TOP2B has a probability of loss-of-function intolerance (pLI) of 1, which suggested disease through haploinsufficiency or partial genetic dominance. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, chimeric or yeast TOP2 constructs carrying the S483L, EE587E, or G633S mutation failed to complement the temperature-sensitive top2-4 allele and did not support recovery of top2-delta haploid spore clones, indicating loss of topoisomerase II function. Haploid strains heterozygous for the mutations grew more slowly, and their nuclear fractions decatenated kinetoplast DNA less effectively than wildtype, indicating a partial dominant-negative effect.

paragraphs.text: In BILU family A from Cyprus, Papapietro et al. (2020) identified a heterozygous c.1453G-C transversion in TOP2B, resulting in an ala485-to-pro (A485P) substitution. It was the only mutation in the coding part of the genome that was absent from the healthy parents, and it arose de novo in the affected woman (II:4), who transmitted it to her affected daughter (III:1). Sanger sequencing showed the same mutation in the patients of family B from France. TOP2B protein levels were reduced in patient T cells, fibroblasts, and iPSCs. In HEK-293 cells, the mutant protein produced a degradation product, which suggested that it was less stable, but it still interacted with TOP2A. Recombinant TOP2B A485P had more than 10-fold reduced DNA relaxation and decatenation activity, and coexpression with wildtype TOP2B lowered decatenation activity. The authors interpreted this as a dominant-negative effect on wildtype TOP2B and TOP2A rather than haploinsufficiency.

paragraphs.text: Broderick et al. (2019) found that Top2b mRNA and protein were expressed more highly in wildtype murine B cells than in T cells. They proposed that the B cell-restricted phenotype reflects a preferential reduction in transcription of long genes when topoisomerase function is lost. They noted that murine B-cell transcription factor genes (EBF 390 kb, Pax5 178 kb, Foxo1 85 kb) are notably longer than T-cell transcription factor genes (Tcf1 30 kb, Notch1 45 kb) or shared ones (Rag1 11 kb, E2A 24 kb). In published ChIP-seq data and etoposide-induced END-seq breaks from murine primary B cells, Top2b, but not Top2a, was present at the promoter and intron 5 enhancer regions of Pax5. This suggested that defective Top2b activity could impair germline transcriptional activity and Igh locus accessibility, with negative effects on V(D)J recombination. Because a bone marrow biopsy had not been clinically indicated in their patients, the stage at which B-cell development fails in humans remained open. However, their murine data suggested a reduced bone marrow B-cell compartment in which the surviving cells had a reduced ability to respond to antigen or general stimuli.

paragraphs.text: Broderick et al. (2019) also generated knockin mice carrying the murine equivalent of the patient EE587E mutation. Homozygotes were not viable. checks.claim: The TOP2B A485P mutation arose de novo in patient II:4 of family A.
checks.evidence_quote: appeared de novo in their affected daughter II:4

checks.claim: Patient II:4 of family A transmitted the TOP2B A485P mutation to her affected daughter III:1.
checks.evidence_quote: then was transmitted to her affected daughter III:1

checks.claim: Patient II:4 of family A had a complete absence of CD19+ cells in bone marrow.
checks.evidence_quote: we studied a bone marrow aspirate of the BILU patient II:4 from family A using multicolor flow cytometry and found a complete absence of any CD19+ cells

checks.claim: Patient II:4 of family A had normal T, NK, and myeloid lineages in bone marrow.
checks.evidence_quote: but normal T, NK and myeloid cell lineages

checks.claim: Sanger sequencing showed the TOP2B A485P mutation in the patients of BILU family B from France.
checks.evidence_quote: we used Sanger sequencing and found that exactly the same mutation was present in patients of family B

checks.claim: The TOP2B A485P mutation was absent from more than 90,000 subjects in gnomAD.
checks.evidence_quote: absent from more than 90,000 subjects in the gnomAD database

checks.claim: TOP2B protein levels were reduced in cells from patients with TOP2B A485P.
checks.evidence_quote: found reduced amounts of the TOP2B protein in patients’ cells in comparison to cells of healthy controls

checks.claim: Recombinant TOP2B A485P had more than 10-fold reduced DNA relaxation and decatenation activity.
checks.evidence_quote: using DNA relaxation and decatenation in vitro assays. We found that enzymatic activities of TOP2BA485P were reduced more than 10 fold

checks.claim: Coexpression of TOP2B A485P with wildtype TOP2B lowered decatenation activity, suggesting a dominant-negative effect.
checks.evidence_quote: co-expression of TOP2BWT and TOP2BA485P proteins resulted in lower decatenation activity than the expression of TOP2BWT alone
checks.explanation: Stated; paper concludes dominant negative effect.
